title: India's Rice Exports Fall as Iran War Chokes Basmati Shipments to the Gulf. 100,000 Tonnes Are Stuck at Indian Ports.
excerpt: Basmati exports to Iran, Iraq, Qatar, and Saudi Arabia have dropped 7 percent since January. Shipping insurance and freight costs have surged. New deals have stalled. And NRIs in the Gulf are starting to feel it at the grocery store.
body:
India's rice exports — the largest in the world — have begun to shrink. The cause is not a failed harvest or a policy reversal. It is the three-month-old war between the United States, Israel, and Iran, which has disrupted the maritime corridor that connects India's rice mills to some of their biggest customers.

## The Numbers Tell the Story

India exported 8.39 million metric tonnes of rice in the first four months of 2026, a 1.3 percent decline from the same period last year, according to two government officials who spoke to Reuters on condition of anonymity. The headline figure understates the severity. Basmati rice exports — the premium variety that accounts for roughly a quarter of India's rice shipments by volume but a far larger share of revenue — fell 7 percent to 2.3 million tonnes.

The decline is concentrated in Gulf-bound shipments. Rice cargoes destined for Iran, Iraq, Qatar, and Saudi Arabia are delayed in transit. According to the All India Rice Exporters Association, roughly 100,000 tonnes of basmati rice are currently stuck at Indian ports, stranded by a combination of skyrocketing shipping insurance, restricted maritime traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, and buyers pulling back from new deals.

## Why the Gulf Matters

India accounts for more than 40 percent of global rice exports — more than the next three largest exporters (Thailand, Vietnam, and Pakistan) combined. But what makes the Gulf market particularly important is the price premium. Basmati commands significantly higher per-tonne prices than the non-basmati rice India ships to Africa and South Asia, meaning the revenue hit from a 7 percent basmati decline far outweighs the modest uptick in non-basmati volumes.

Iran was India's single largest market for basmati rice until last year, when Saudi Arabia overtook it. Both are now affected by the same war. The shipping lanes that Indian exporters have relied on for decades are no longer functioning normally.

## The Ripple Effects

The disruption is not just a headline for trade ministries. It is already being felt in at least three places that matter to the Indian diaspora.

**In the Gulf**, where an estimated 8.5 million Indians live and work, the supply squeeze is beginning to push up retail prices for basmati rice — a pantry staple in NRI kitchens from Dubai to Doha. Indian grocery stores in the UAE have reported intermittent shortages of popular basmati brands, with some switching to Pakistani substitutes.

**In India**, the export slowdown is depressing domestic rice prices, which have already fallen more than 5 percent this year despite a record harvest. For farmers in Punjab, Haryana, and Uttar Pradesh — the heartland of basmati cultivation — the timing is brutal. Input costs have risen with global fuel prices, but the export market that historically absorbed surplus production is now frozen.

**In Africa and South Asia**, freight cost increases are rippling outward. India's non-basmati rice shipments to Bangladesh, Benin, Ivory Coast, Guinea, and Cameroon have held roughly steady, but exporters say new deal-making has slowed as buyers calculate whether the war premium on shipping makes Indian rice competitive against Thai and Vietnamese alternatives.

## What Comes Next

One New Delhi-based exporter told Reuters that shipments were expected to remain below typical levels until the Iran war ends. That is a significant qualifier. There is no ceasefire in sight — U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said this week that negotiations could "take a few days," even as fresh strikes were being reported.

India's government has so far resisted calls to intervene directly in the rice export market. But the pressure is building. Domestic rice prices are falling, farmers are absorbing losses, and the foreign exchange earnings from basmati — India's most valuable agricultural export — are declining at exactly the moment the rupee is under pressure from a $98 oil price.

For the Indian diaspora in the Gulf, the disruption is still manageable — an inconvenience, not a crisis. But if the Strait of Hormuz remains contested through the monsoon season, the world's most important rice trade corridor will have been effectively severed for six months. And the consequences will be measured in more than just tonnes.
nri_angle: NRIs in the Gulf are facing basmati rice shortages and price hikes as the Iran war disrupts India's rice exports. 100,000 tonnes are stuck at Indian ports, and the supply squeeze is hitting Indian grocery stores from Dubai to Doha.
